kubler_ross_stages.name: Kübler-Ross Model (Five Stages of Grief)
kubler_ross_stages.description: Originally developed for those facing terminal illness, widely applied to grief. Important: stages are NOT linear or universal - people may skip stages, revisit them, or experience multiple simultaneously.

stages.name: Denial
stages.description: A defense mechanism that buffers the immediate shock. Not about denying the death happened, but struggling to accept the new reality.
manifestations: Expecting them to walk through the door
supportive_responses: It can take time for reality to sink in. That's normal.
The mind protects us by absorbing loss slowly.
There's no rush to 'accept' anything right now.

stages.name: Anger
stages.description: As denial fades, pain emerges. Anger is the emotional outlet - at the situation, medical system, the deceased, God, oneself, or the world.
manifestations: Resentment toward those who haven't experienced loss
supportive_responses: Anger is a completely valid part of grief.
It's okay to be angry - at them, at the world, at yourself.
Anger often comes from love and from the unfairness of loss.

stages.name: Bargaining
stages.description: Dwelling on 'what if' and 'if only' statements. Attempting to negotiate, often with a higher power, to reverse or lessen the loss.
manifestations: 'What if I had called that day?'
'If only they had gone to the doctor sooner'
Replaying scenarios where the outcome changes
Guilt about things said or unsaid
supportive_responses: It's natural to search for ways this could have been different.
The 'what ifs' are the mind trying to find control in an uncontrollable situation.
Going over these scenarios doesn't mean you failed them.

stages.name: Depression
stages.description: Deep sadness as the full weight of loss settles in. Not clinical depression, but appropriate sadness for a significant loss.
supportive_responses: This sadness is not a sign of weakness - it's the measure of your love.
It's okay to not be okay right now.
Grief takes energy. Being exhausted makes sense.

stages.name: Acceptance
stages.description: Not being 'okay' with the loss, but acknowledging the reality and learning to live with it. Finding new meaning while honoring the relationship.
manifestations: Acknowledging the permanence of the loss
Beginning to plan and look forward
Integrating the loss into one's life story
supportive_responses: Acceptance doesn't mean forgetting or 'moving on.'
Finding peace doesn't mean you love them less.
You're not leaving them behind - you're carrying them with you differently.

important_notes: Stages don't follow a linear progression
People can be in multiple stages simultaneously
There is no 'correct' timeline for grief
Revisiting earlier stages is normal and healthy

wordens_tasks.name: Worden's Four Tasks of Mourning
wordens_tasks.description: An active framework that views grief as work to be done, giving mourners agency in their healing process.

tasks.task: Accept the reality of the loss
tasks.description: Coming to terms with the fact that the person is dead and will not return. Both intellectual and emotional acceptance.
what_helps: Viewing the body or attending the funeral
Talking about the death and the person
Using past tense when referring to them

tasks.description: Allowing oneself to feel the full range of emotions without numbing or avoiding them.
what_helps: Expressing feelings through talking, writing, or art
Acknowledging that pain is proportional to love

tasks.task: Adjust to a world without the deceased
tasks.description: Adapting to life in which the deceased is missing - practically, emotionally, and spiritually.
what_helps: Learning new skills they used to handle

tasks.task: Find an enduring connection while embarking on new life
tasks.description: Finding a way to maintain a bond with the deceased while reinvesting in living.
what_helps: Creating rituals to honor their memory
Carrying forward their values or traditions
Finding meaning in the relationship that continues

dual_process_model.name: Dual Process Model of Coping with Bereavement
dual_process_model.description: Developed by Stroebe and Schut. Healthy grieving involves oscillation between loss-oriented and restoration-oriented coping.

loss_oriented.description: Focus on the loss itself and emotional processing

restoration_oriented.description: Focus on secondary changes and life adjustments

dual_process_model.key_insight: Both are necessary. People naturally oscillate between them. Too much of either is problematic. Some days are for feeling; some are for doing. Both serve healing.

continuing_bonds.name: Continuing Bonds Theory
continuing_bonds.description: Developed by Klass, Silverman, and Nickman. Challenges the idea that grief's goal is 'letting go.' Instead, the relationship transforms but continues.
principles: The bond with the deceased doesn't end with death
Maintaining connection is healthy and normal
Bonds are maintained through memory, linking objects, rituals, and legacy
healthy_continuing_bonds: Celebrating their birthday or death anniversary
Feeling their presence in certain moments
Seeking their guidance or imagining their advice

5_4_3_2_1_method.name: 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding
5_4_3_2_1_method.when_to_use: During overwhelming emotions, panic, dissociation, or feeling untethered
instructions: Name 5 things you can SEE around you
Name 4 things you can TOUCH or feel
5_4_3_2_1_method.why_it_works: Engages the senses to anchor you in the present moment, interrupting the spiral of overwhelming emotion

box_breathing.name: Box Breathing (4-4-4-4)
box_breathing.when_to_use: Anxiety, racing thoughts, difficulty calming down
box_breathing.why_it_works: Activates the parasympathetic nervous system, signaling safety to the body

feet_on_floor.name: Feet on Floor
instructions: Press your feet firmly into the floor
Notice the sensation of the ground beneath you
Feel the support of the earth holding you up
You are here. You are real. You are safe.

cold_water.name: Cold Water Reset
instructions: Run cold water over your wrists
Hold ice cubes in your hands
Splash cold water on your face
Feel the physical sensation as an anchor

for_sadness: What do I miss most about them today?
If I could tell them one thing, what would it be?
What memory brings me comfort right now?
What would they want me to know in this moment?
for_anger: What am I really angry about?
What feels unfair about this situation?
If I could yell into a void, what would I say?
What need isn't being met right now?
for_guilt: What would I say to a friend feeling this same guilt?
What did I do right in my relationship with them?
What would they say to me about this guilt?
for_anxiety: What am I afraid of right now?
What's the worst case scenario, and could I survive it?
What's one small thing I can control today?
What would help me feel even a little safer?
for_memory_keeping: Describe their laugh, voice, or the way they walked.
What was their favorite thing to do?
What did they teach me that I still carry?
Describe a perfectly ordinary day with them.
for_moving_forward: What would they want for my life?
How do I want to honor their memory?
What parts of them do I see in myself?
What can I do today that they would be proud of?

basics: Eat something - even if you're not hungry
Sleep when you can - grief is exhausting
Move your body gently - even a short walk
Go outside briefly - sunlight and fresh air help
permission_slips: You can say no to things
You can take a break from grief
You can laugh and still be grieving
You can grieve in your own way and timeline

crisis_indicators.description: Immediate safety concerns requiring crisis resources
indicators: Suicidal ideation or plans
Self-harm thoughts or behaviors
Wanting to join the deceased
Feeling like a burden to others
Giving away possessions
Saying goodbye to people
Stockpiling medications
Researching methods of self-harm
crisis_indicators.response: Provide 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline immediately

complicated_grief_signs.description: Signs that grief may benefit from professional support
indicators: Inability to accept the death after extended time
Persistent and intrusive longing that doesn't ease
Feeling that life is meaningless without them
Avoiding anything associated with the deceased OR obsessive focus
Intense bitterness or anger that doesn't diminish
Difficulty trusting others since the death
Feeling emotionally numb for extended periods
Inability to function in daily life after several months
complicated_grief_signs.response: Gently suggest grief counseling when appropriate

depression_vs_grief.description: While sadness is normal in grief, watch for signs of clinical depression
grief_typical: Sadness comes in waves, often triggered by reminders
Can still experience moments of joy
Yearning is for the specific person lost
depression_signs: Guilt not related to the deceased
Suicidal thoughts (not just passive wishing to join them)
Complete inability to function after extended time

indicators: Using alcohol or drugs to numb pain daily
Increasing tolerance - needing more to cope
Unable to face grief sober
Others expressing concern about substance use
Substances interfering with daily functioning
substance_abuse_concerns.response: Acknowledge this is common but concerning; suggest professional support

physical_symptoms: Difficulty sleeping or sleeping too much
emotional_range: Moments of peace or even joy
social_changes: Difficulty relating to those who haven't experienced loss
Needing support but not knowing how to ask
